analysis.one_liner: Directs the President to force emergency production of masks, tests, and vaccines at fair prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 26, 2020 with 4 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and died there without a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the President, within one day of enactment, to use the Defense Production Act — a WWII-era law letting the government direct factories to make goods needed for national defense — to require companies to produce COVID-19 supplies like N95 masks, test kits, and vaccines. It would have set a fair price for those goods, shipped them to states based on governors' requests and population, and put leftovers into the federal stockpile. It was referred to committee the day it was introduced and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Healthcare workers, nursing home residents, and the general public, who faced shortages of masks, gowns, and tests during the 2020 pandemic; state governors, who would have had a federal channel to request supplies rather than bidding against each other and other countries on the open market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Healthcare workers and the public facing mask and test shortages

how_it_helps.text: Would have required the President to identify private factory capacity and compel emergency production of N95 masks, face shields, diagnostic tests, and vaccines, addressing the severe shortages of these items in 2020 [S2][S3].
Would have set a fair and reasonable price for supplies produced under the order, preventing government purchase orders from inflating prices or rewarding the highest bidder [S3].

Would have allocated supplies to states based on governors' requests and each state's population, replacing the 2020 free-for-all in which states bid against each other and the federal government for the same goods [S2][S3].
Would have sent unused supplies to the Strategic National Stockpile, so the government would be better prepared for the next emergency [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Defense Production Act Fund — federal taxpayer money — would pay for the production, and manufacturers of medical supplies would have to fill compulsory orders at government-set prices rather than selling at whatever price the market allowed.

drawbacks.text: Mandating production at government-set 'fair and reasonable' prices can discourage manufacturers from expanding capacity or from bidding for the contracts, since they could earn more selling elsewhere [S3].

The bill gave the President one day after enactment to issue sweeping production orders and put the cost on the existing Defense Production Act Fund, with no new appropriation — a design that leaned heavily on the administration's own willingness to act and on money that might not stretch far enough [S3].

A centralized federal allocation based on governors' requests and population could misallocate supplies in a fast-moving epidemic compared with allocation based on real-time case counts and hospital strain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: In the middle of a pandemic with documented mask and test shortages, compelling factories to run at government-set prices is a low-cost intervention compared with the human toll of shortages. The bill's weaknesses are real but modest: it relied on an existing fund rather than new money and on the President's own diligence, and price-setting carries some risk of under-supply. On balance the costs are small next to the benefit of getting protective equipment and tests to the states that needed them.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on May 26, 2020, about two months into the pandemic, with Reps. Blunt Rochester and Crist as original cosponsors [S3].
Four Democrats in total cosponsored the bill, all from the House [S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the 116th Congress, which ended January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical supply manufacturers and distributors were better off because the bill died: no government order could compel them to produce masks, tests, and vaccines at capped prices, leaving them free to sell at market rates during a shortage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Medical supply makers free to sell at market prices

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so no position can be measured; its 5 sponsors and cosponsors were all Democrats, and no Republican supported it on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have forced these companies to accept production orders for masks, face shields, and test materials at government-set prices. During a shortage, that meant giving up the ability to sell scarce goods to the highest bidder — which is precisely why the public needed the bill and the industry benefited from its death.
Test makers and their reagent suppliers would have been subject to the same compelled production at capped prices, limiting profits on tests during the pandemic surge.

Once the FDA approved a COVID-19 vaccine, the bill would have required its emergency production at a fair price and routed it to states by population — guaranteeing a buyer but capping pricing and dictating distribution.
